```{r as-style, include=FALSE}
# ---- Presentation: 95% confidence intervals instead of significance stars ----
# These local definitions override the shared helpers for this paper only (R/helpers.R is untouched).
stars <- function(p) ""
# Never print a negative zero ("-0.0", "-0.00"); otherwise as the shared helper.
.fmt <- function(x, d, suffix = "") {
  x <- suppressWarnings(as.numeric(x)); x[!is.finite(x)] <- NA
  s <- sub("^-(0\\.?0*)$", "\\1", formatC(x, format = "f", digits = d, big.mark = ","))
  ifelse(is.na(x), "--", paste0(s, suffix))
}
f3 <- function(x) .fmt(x, 3)
ci_txt <- function(lo, hi, d = 1) paste0("CI ", .fmt(lo, d), " to ", .fmt(hi, d))
est_se <- function(e, digits = 1, unit = "minutes") {
  if (is.null(e$est) || is.na(e$est)) return("not estimable")
  paste0(.fmt(e$est, digits), if (nzchar(unit)) paste0(" ", unit) else "",
         " (", ci_txt(e$est - 1.96 * e$se, e$est + 1.96 * e$se, digits), ")")
}
diff_txt <- function(e, more = "more", less = "less", digits = 1, unit = "minutes") {
  if (is.null(e$est) || is.na(e$est)) return("[not estimable]")
  paste0(.fmt(abs(e$est), digits), if (nzchar(unit)) paste0(" ", unit) else "", " ", more_less(e$est, more, less),
         " (", ci_txt(e$est - 1.96 * e$se, e$est + 1.96 * e$se, digits), ")")
}
diff_pp <- function(e, more = "higher", less = "lower", digits = 1) {
  if (is.null(e$est) || is.na(e$est)) return("not estimable")
  paste0(.fmt(100 * abs(e$est), digits), " percentage points ", more_less(e$est, more, less),
         " (", ci_txt(100 * (e$est - 1.96 * e$se), 100 * (e$est + 1.96 * e$se), digits), ")")
}
ci_cell <- function(k, d = 2) if (is.null(k$est) || is.na(k$est)) "--" else
  paste0("[", .fmt(k$est - 1.96 * k$se, d), ", ", .fmt(k$est + 1.96 * k$se, d), "]")
nw <- function(n) { w <- c("zero", "one", "two", "three", "four", "five", "six", "seven", "eight", "nine", "ten")
  n <- suppressWarnings(as.integer(n)); if (length(n) == 1 && !is.na(n) && n >= 0 && n <= 10) w[n + 1] else .fmt(n, 0) }
```

```{r sample}
R <- CODE$relation
HEADLVL <- unname(R[c("head", "spouse")])
JUNIOR  <- unname(R[c("married_child", "child_spouse")])
PARENT  <- unname(R["parent_or_inlaw"])

# ---- Household-level counts (added to pd BEFORE any subsetting) ----------------
hhx <- pd[, .(
  n_junior_mw  = sum(female == 1 & married == 1 & rel %in% JUNIOR & age >= 15 & age <= 49),
  n_head_mw    = sum(female == 1 & married == 1 & rel %in% HEADLVL & age >= 18 & age <= 49),
  n_mw_18_49   = sum(female == 1 & married == 1 & age >= 18 & age <= 49),
  n_adult_women = sum(female == 1 & age >= 15),
  hh_cc_all    = sum(care_child[age >= 15])
), by = hh_id]
pd[hhx, on = "hh_id", names(hhx)[-1] := mget(paste0("i.", names(hhx)[-1]))]

# ---- Candidate mothers ----------------------------------------------------------
# Married women 18-49 whose roster position identifies the generation above them.
elig0 <- pd[female == 1 & married == 1 & age >= 18 & age <= 49 & rel %in% c(HEADLVL, JUNIOR)]
elig0[, junior := as.integer(rel %in% JUNIOR)]
# A head-level woman who lives with a married child's couple of childbearing age is,
# in a household with a child under six, most likely that child's grandmother rather
# than its mother. She is excluded from the mother sample and enters the
# older-generation sample below.
n_u6_pool   <- elig0[!is.na(hh_n_under6) & hh_n_under6 > 0, .N]
n_u6_dropgm <- elig0[!is.na(hh_n_under6) & hh_n_under6 > 0 & junior == 0 & n_junior_mw > 0, .N]
elig <- elig0[!(junior == 0 & n_junior_mw > 0)]

# ---- Link each mother to the older generation's own diaries -----------------------
older <- pd[, .(hh_id, o_pid = pid, o_rel = rel, o_female = female, o_age = age,
                o_cc = care_child, o_cc_act = care_child_active, o_cc_pas = care_child_passive,
                o_dom = unpaid_domestic, o_emp = employment, o_ft = free_time,
                o_employed = employed)]
lk <- rbind(
  merge(elig[junior == 0, .(pid, hh_id)], older[o_rel == PARENT], by = "hh_id", allow.cartesian = TRUE),
  merge(elig[junior == 1, .(pid, hh_id)], older[o_rel %in% HEADLVL & o_age >= 40], by = "hh_id",
        allow.cartesian = TRUE))
n_self_links <- lk[o_pid == pid, .N]          # must be 0: no mother is her own grandmother
lk <- lk[o_pid != pid]
og <- lk[, .(
  gm_n = sum(o_female == 1), gf_n = sum(o_female == 0),
  gm_care_child = sum(o_cc * (o_female == 1)), gm_cc_act = sum(o_cc_act * (o_female == 1)),
  gm_cc_pas = sum(o_cc_pas * (o_female == 1)), gm_domestic = sum(o_dom * (o_female == 1)),
  gm_employment = sum(o_emp * (o_female == 1)), gm_free_time = sum(o_ft * (o_female == 1)),
  gm_employed = as.integer(any(o_female == 1 & o_employed %in% 1)),
  gm_age_min = if (any(o_female == 1)) min(o_age[o_female == 1]) else NA_real_,
  gf_care_child = sum(o_cc * (o_female == 0))
), by = pid]

Mo <- merge(elig, og, by = "pid", all.x = TRUE)
zero <- c("gm_n", "gf_n", "gm_care_child", "gm_cc_act", "gm_cc_pas", "gm_domestic",
          "gm_employment", "gm_free_time", "gm_employed", "gf_care_child")
for (v in zero) Mo[is.na(get(v)), (v) := 0]
# Agreement with the shared panel's count of older-generation women (should be 100%).
share_link_consistent <- Mo[, mean(gm_n == n_older_gen_women, na.rm = TRUE)]

Mo[, `:=`(
  gm_any   = as.integer(gm_n > 0),
  gf_any   = as.integer(gf_n > 0),
  gp_any   = as.integer(gm_n + gf_n > 0),
  husband  = as.integer(!is.na(spouse_pid)),
  spouse_emp = fifelse(is.na(spouse_employed), 0L, as.integer(spouse_employed)),
  father_cc = fifelse(is.na(spouse_care_child), 0, spouse_care_child),
  special  = as.integer(special_care %in% CODE$yes_no["yes"]),
  kids_6_17 = fcoalesce(as.integer(own_kids_6_17), 0L),
  kids_unknown = as.integer(is.na(own_kids_6_17)),
  sole     = as.integer(n_mw_18_49 == 1),
  any_cc   = as.integer(care_child > 0),
  edu_hi   = as.integer(edu_tier %in% names(CODE$edu_tier)[3:4])
)]
Mo[, spouse_edu_f := factor(fifelse(husband == 0, "No linked husband",
                                    fifelse(is.na(spouse_edu_tier), "Unknown", as.character(spouse_edu_tier))))]
Mo[, `:=`(
  gm_only = as.integer(gm_any == 1 & gf_any == 0),
  gf_only = as.integer(gm_any == 0 & gf_any == 1),
  gp_both = as.integer(gm_any == 1 & gf_any == 1),
  gm_young = as.integer(gm_any == 1 & gm_age_min < 60),
  gm_old   = as.integer(gm_any == 1 & gm_age_min >= 60),
  gm_work  = as.integer(gm_any == 1 & gm_employed == 1),
  gm_nowork = as.integer(gm_any == 1 & gm_employed == 0),
  n_other_women = pmax(n_adult_women - 1 - gm_n, 0),
  hh_care_mo_gm = care_child + gm_care_child,
  others_cc = pmax(hh_cc_all - care_child - father_cc - gm_care_child - gf_care_child, 0),
  gp_lab = factor(ifelse(gm_any == 1, "Grandmother present", "No grandmother"),
                  levels = c("No grandmother", "Grandmother present"))
)]

MY <- Mo[!is.na(hh_n_under6) & hh_n_under6 > 0]                     # analysis sample
MP <- Mo[!is.na(hh_n_under6) & hh_n_under6 == 0 & !is.na(youngest_own_kid) &
           youngest_own_kid >= 6 & youngest_own_kid <= 14]           # placebo sample
MY[, multi_u6 := as.integer(hh_n_under6 >= 2)]

# ---- Specification ----------------------------------------------------------------
CV <- c("i(age_band)", "i(edu_tier)", "urban", "i(mpce_quintile)", "kids_6_17", "kids_unknown",
        "hh_n_under6", "hh_n_6_14", "i(spouse_edu_f)", "spouse_emp", "i(social_group_f)",
        "i(religion_f)", "special", "proxy_report")
f <- function(y, x = "gm_any", d = MY, extra = NULL)
  reg(as.formula(paste(y, "~", x, "+", ctrl(d, c(CV, extra)), fe(d))), d)

# Difference between two coefficients of one model, with SE.
dcoef <- function(m, a, b) {
  if (is.null(m) || !all(c(a, b) %in% names(coef(m)))) return(list(est = NA, se = NA, p = NA))
  v <- vcov(m); d <- unname(coef(m)[a] - coef(m)[b])
  s <- sqrt(v[a, a] + v[b, b] - 2 * v[a, b]); list(est = d, se = s, p = 2 * pnorm(-abs(d / s)))
}
cell <- function(k, d = 2) .fmt(k$est, d)
# Difference of estimates from two separate regressions; SE ignores their covariance
# (conservative when the covariance is positive, as within households and FSUs).
ddiff <- function(a, b) {
  if (is.na(a$est) || is.na(b$est)) return(list(est = NA, se = NA, p = NA))
  d <- a$est - b$est; s <- sqrt(a$se^2 + b$se^2); list(est = d, se = s, p = 2 * pnorm(-abs(d / s)))
}
cse  <- function(k, d = 2) if (is.null(k$est) || is.na(k$est)) "--" else
  paste0(.fmt(k$est, d), " ", ci_cell(k, d))

outs <- c("care_child", "care_child_active", "care_child_passive", "sec_care_child",
          "unpaid_domestic", "dom_food", "care_dep_adult", "employment", "free_time", "sleep")
out_lab <- c(care_child = "Childcare (primary)", care_child_active = "\\quad Active childcare",
             care_child_passive = "\\quad Passive childcare (minding)",
             sec_care_child = "Childcare as secondary activity", unpaid_domestic = "Unpaid domestic work",
             dom_food = "\\quad of which food and meals", care_dep_adult = "Care of dependent adults",
             employment = "Employment (incl. travel)", free_time = "Free time", sleep = "Sleep",
             employed = "Employed (usual status, share)")
m_gm <- setNames(lapply(c(outs, "employed"), f), c(outs, "employed"))
e <- function(y, t = "gm_any", ml = m_gm) coef_of(ml[[y]], t)

k_cc <- e("care_child"); k_act <- e("care_child_active"); k_pas <- e("care_child_passive")
k_sec <- e("sec_care_child"); k_dom <- e("unpaid_domestic"); k_food <- e("dom_food")
k_adult <- e("care_dep_adult"); k_emp <- e("employment"); k_ft <- e("free_time")
k_sleep <- e("sleep"); k_lfp <- e("employed")
k_all <- coef_of(f("hh_cc_all"), "gm_any")
k_fa  <- coef_of(f("father_cc", d = MY[husband == 1]), "gm_any")

# ---- Descriptives -----------------------------------------------------------------
n_my <- nrow(MY); n_mp <- nrow(MP)
share_gm  <- wmean(MY$gm_any, MY$weight)
share_gf  <- wmean(MY$gf_any, MY$weight)
share_gfo <- wmean(MY$gf_only, MY$weight)
share_jun <- wmean(MY$junior, MY$weight)
share_dil <- if (nrow(MY[junior == 1])) wmean(MY[junior == 1]$rel == R["child_spouse"], MY[junior == 1]$weight) else NA
share_jun_gm <- if (nrow(MY[gm_any == 1])) wmean(MY[gm_any == 1]$junior, MY[gm_any == 1]$weight) else NA
share_hus <- wmean(MY$husband, MY$weight)
share_sole <- wmean(MY$sole, MY$weight)
n_jun_nogm <- MY[junior == 1 & gm_any == 0, .N]; n_jun_gm <- MY[junior == 1 & gm_any == 1, .N]
n_head_nogm <- MY[junior == 0 & gm_any == 0, .N]; n_head_gm <- MY[junior == 0 & gm_any == 1, .N]
mo_cc0 <- est_mean(MY[gm_any == 0], "care_child"); mo_cc1 <- est_mean(MY[gm_any == 1], "care_child")
gm_cc  <- est_mean(MY[gm_any == 1], "gm_care_child")
gm_dom <- est_mean(MY[gm_any == 1], "gm_domestic")
gm_empm <- est_mean(MY[gm_any == 1], "gm_employment")
gm_age_med <- if (nrow(MY[gm_any == 1])) median(MY[gm_any == 1]$gm_age_min) else NA
share_gm_young <- if (nrow(MY[gm_any == 1])) wmean(MY[gm_any == 1]$gm_young, MY[gm_any == 1]$weight) else NA
share_gm_work <- if (nrow(MY[gm_any == 1])) wmean(MY[gm_any == 1]$gm_work, MY[gm_any == 1]$weight) else NA
gm_share_cc <- with(MY[gm_any == 1], sum(weight * gm_care_child) / sum(weight * (gm_care_child + care_child)))

# ---- Heterogeneity ------------------------------------------------------------------
MIN_CELL <- 30   # minimum mothers with and without a grandmother for a split to be reported
het <- function(d, y = "care_child") {
  ok <- d[gm_any == 1, .N] >= MIN_CELL && d[gm_any == 0, .N] >= MIN_CELL
  if (!ok) return(list(est = NA, se = NA, p = NA, n = nrow(d), ok = FALSE))
  c(coef_of(f(y, d = d), "gm_any"), n = nrow(d), ok = TRUE)
}
splits <- list(head = MY[junior == 0], jun = MY[junior == 1], urb = MY[urban == 1], rur = MY[urban == 0],
               elo = MY[edu_hi == 0], ehi = MY[edu_hi == 1], one = MY[multi_u6 == 0], two = MY[multi_u6 == 1])
H     <- lapply(splits, het)
H_emp <- lapply(splits, het, y = "employment")
jun_estimable <- isTRUE(H$jun$ok) && !is.na(H$jun$est)

# Who is the grandparent: age (health proxy), employment, sex
m_age  <- lapply(c(cc = "care_child", emp = "employment"), function(y) f(y, "gm_young + gm_old"))
m_work <- lapply(c(cc = "care_child", emp = "employment"), function(y) f(y, "gm_nowork + gm_work"))
m_sex  <- lapply(c(cc = "care_child", emp = "employment"), function(y) f(y, "gm_only + gf_only + gp_both"))
A <- list(
  young = lapply(m_age, coef_of, "gm_young"), old = lapply(m_age, coef_of, "gm_old"),
  dage = lapply(m_age, dcoef, "gm_young", "gm_old"),
  nowork = lapply(m_work, coef_of, "gm_nowork"), work = lapply(m_work, coef_of, "gm_work"),
  dwork = lapply(m_work, dcoef, "gm_nowork", "gm_work"),
  gmo = lapply(m_sex, coef_of, "gm_only"), gfo = lapply(m_sex, coef_of, "gf_only"),
  both = lapply(m_sex, coef_of, "gp_both"), dsex = lapply(m_sex, dcoef, "gm_only", "gf_only"))

# ---- Placebo: youngest own child aged 6-14, no child under six ------------------------
pl_outs <- c("care_child", "care_child_active", "care_child_passive", "unpaid_domestic", "employment")
PL <- lapply(setNames(pl_outs, pl_outs), function(y) list(
  u6 = coef_of(m_gm[[y]], "gm_any"),
  pl = coef_of(f(y, d = MP), "gm_any"),
  dd = NULL))
for (y in pl_outs) PL[[y]]$dd <- ddiff(PL[[y]]$u6, PL[[y]]$pl)
k_pl <- PL$care_child$pl; k_dd <- PL$care_child$dd; k_pl_emp <- PL$employment$pl

# ---- The older generation's own trade-offs ---------------------------------------------
# Members aged 45-80 in the generation above a married woman of childbearing age:
# head/spouse living with a married child's couple, or parent/in-law of the head living
# with a head-level couple. Treatment: a child under six in the household.
OG <- pd[age >= 45 & age <= 80 & !is.na(hh_n_under6) &
           ((rel %in% HEADLVL & n_junior_mw > 0) | (rel == PARENT & n_head_mw > 0))]
OG[, `:=`(young_gc = as.integer(hh_n_under6 > 0),
          special = as.integer(special_care %in% CODE$yes_no["yes"]))]
CVo <- c("i(age_band)", "i(edu_tier)", "urban", "i(mpce_quintile)", "married", "hh_n_6_14",
         "i(social_group_f)", "i(religion_f)", "special", "proxy_report")
fo <- function(y, d, x = "young_gc") reg(as.formula(paste(y, "~", x, "+", ctrl(d, CVo), fe(d))), d)
og_outs <- c("care_child", "care_child_active", "care_child_passive", "unpaid_domestic",
             "employment", "employed", "free_time", "sleep")
OGW <- OG[female == 1]; OGM <- OG[female == 0]
T_gm <- lapply(setNames(og_outs, og_outs), function(y) coef_of(fo(y, OGW), "young_gc"))
T_gf <- lapply(setNames(og_outs, og_outs), function(y) coef_of(fo(y, OGM), "young_gc"))
T_dd <- lapply(setNames(og_outs, og_outs), function(y) ddiff(T_gm[[y]], T_gf[[y]]))
n_ogw <- nrow(OGW); n_ogm <- nrow(OGM)
t_cc <- T_gm$care_child; t_emp <- T_gm$employment; t_ft <- T_gm$free_time; t_dom <- T_gm$unpaid_domestic
t_lfp <- T_gm$employed; t_sleep <- T_gm$sleep; tf_cc <- T_gf$care_child; td_cc <- T_dd$care_child
tf_emp <- T_gf$employment

# ---- Robustness -------------------------------------------------------------------------
m1 <- m_gm$care_child
ob <- NA_real_; obe <- NA_real_
if (!is.null(m1)) {
  m0 <- reg(care_child ~ gm_any, MY[obs(m1)])
  ob <- tryCatch(oster_beta(m0, m1, "gm_any"), error = function(e) NA_real_)
}
if (!is.null(m_gm$employment)) {
  m0e <- reg(employment ~ gm_any, MY[obs(m_gm$employment)])
  obe <- tryCatch(oster_beta(m0e, m_gm$employment, "gm_any"), error = function(e) NA_real_)
}
unw <- tryCatch(coef_of(feols(as.formula(paste("care_child ~ gm_any +", ctrl(MY, CV), fe(MY))),
                              MY, cluster = ~fsu), "gm_any"), error = function(e) list(est = NA, se = NA, p = NA))
RB <- list(
  "Baseline" = k_cc,
  "Only married woman aged 18--49 in the household" = coef_of(f("care_child", d = MY[sole == 1]), "gm_any"),
  "Head-level mothers only (head or spouse of head)" = coef_of(f("care_child", d = MY[junior == 0]), "gm_any"),
  "Mothers with a linked husband only" = coef_of(f("care_child", d = MY[husband == 1]), "gm_any"),
  "Self-reported diaries only" = coef_of(f("care_child", d = MY[proxy_report == 0]), "gm_any"),
  "Controlling for other women aged 15+" = coef_of(f("care_child", extra = "n_other_women"), "gm_any"),
  "Controlling for household size" = coef_of(f("care_child", extra = "hh_size"), "gm_any"),
  "Controlling for mother's generation (junior)" = coef_of(f("care_child", extra = "junior"), "gm_any"),
  "Unweighted" = unw,
  "Any grandparent instead of grandmother" = coef_of(f("care_child", "gp_any"), "gp_any"))
k_any_cc <- coef_of(f("any_cc"), "gm_any")
rb_est <- vapply(RB, function(k) as.numeric(k$est), numeric(1))
rb_sign_stable <- all(!is.na(rb_est)) && (all(rb_est < 0) || all(rb_est > 0))
rb_range <- range(rb_est, na.rm = TRUE)

# ---- Verdicts (drive every results-dependent sentence) ----------------------------------
sub_child <- is_neg(k_cc)
cc_up     <- is_pos(k_cc)
emp_up    <- is_pos(k_emp)
emp_down  <- is_neg(k_emp)
lfp_up    <- is_pos(k_lfp)
dom_up    <- is_pos(k_dom)
dom_down  <- is_neg(k_dom)
ft_up     <- is_pos(k_ft)
hh_more   <- is_pos(k_all)
hh_less   <- is_neg(k_all)
pas_only  <- is_neg(k_pas) && !is_neg(k_act)
act_too   <- is_neg(k_act)
pl_null   <- !is_sig(k_pl)
# Significant changes in grandmothers' other activities with a young grandchild
og_names <- c(unpaid_domestic = "domestic work", employment = "paid work", free_time = "free time", sleep = "sleep")
og_neg <- unname(og_names[vapply(names(og_names), function(y) is_neg(T_gm[[y]]), logical(1))])
og_pos <- unname(og_names[vapply(names(og_names), function(y) is_pos(T_gm[[y]]), logical(1))])
and_list <- function(x) if (length(x) <= 1) paste(x, collapse = "") else paste(paste(x[-length(x)], collapse = ", "), "and", x[length(x)])
gm_cost_cc  <- is_pos(t_cc)
gm_cost_emp <- is_neg(t_emp) || is_neg(t_lfp)
gm_cost_ft  <- is_neg(t_ft)
gf_cc_up    <- is_pos(tf_cc)
gf_less     <- is_pos(td_cc)
age_grad    <- is_sig(A$dage$cc)
work_grad   <- is_sig(A$dwork$cc)
sex_grad    <- is_sig(A$dsex$cc)
oster_same_sign <- !is.na(ob) && !is.na(k_cc$est) && sign(ob) == sign(k_cc$est)

# ---- Additional derived quantities ---------------------------
ci_incl0 <- function(k) isTRUE(!is.na(k$est) && (k$est - 1.96 * k$se) <= 0 && (k$est + 1.96 * k$se) >= 0)
cilo <- function(k, d = 1) .fmt(k$est - 1.96 * k$se, d)
cihi <- function(k, d = 1) .fmt(k$est + 1.96 * k$se, d)
emp_sign_differs <- length(unique(sign(na.omit(c(A$gmo$emp$est, A$both$emp$est, A$gfo$emp$est))))) > 1
cap_pattern <- age_grad && isTRUE(A$dage$cc$est > 0) && work_grad && isTRUE(A$dwork$cc$est < 0)
hx <- function(k) if (isTRUE(k$ok) && !is.na(k$est)) est_se(k) else "not estimable"
base_cc <- wmean(MY[gm_any == 0]$care_child, MY[gm_any == 0]$weight)
# Cross-check of the roster count against the household-size variable in the household file
share_roster_hh <- tryCatch({
  u <- pd[!duplicated(hh_id)]
  if (all(c("hh_size", "hh_n_roster") %in% names(u))) mean(u$hh_size == u$hh_n_roster, na.rm = TRUE) else NA_real_
}, error = function(e) NA_real_)
```

\begin{abstract}
Do coresident grandmothers relieve mothers of childcare, and what do they give up? Same-day time diaries from India's Time Use Survey 2024 cover both generations in each household. I compare `r fn(n_my)` married mothers of children under six, `r pctx(share_gm, 0)` of whom live with a grandmother, and `r fn(n_ogw)` women and `r fn(n_ogm)` men aged 45 to 80 in the generation above them. The innovation is to measure grandmothers' own time and to assign grandmothers and young children correctly in rosters without parent identifiers. Grandmothers living with a young grandchild report `r f1(t_cc$est)` minutes more childcare a day`r iff(length(og_neg) > 0, paste0(" and less ", and_list(og_neg)), "")`. `r iff(ci_incl0(k_cc) && ci_incl0(k_emp), "Mothers' childcare and paid work differ little between households with and without a grandmother, the confidence intervals include zero, and the estimates are fragile.", "Mothers' childcare and paid work differ between households with and without a grandmother, and the estimates are fragile across specifications.")` The contribution is to show that grandmother care is a costly transfer of older women's time, while its benefit for mothers' work is not established.
\end{abstract}

\noindent\textbf{Keywords:} grandparents $\cdot$ childcare $\cdot$ three-generation households $\cdot$ patrilocality $\cdot$ time use $\cdot$ India

\noindent\textbf{JEL Classification:} D13 $\cdot$ J13 $\cdot$ J22


# Introduction

Grandparents are a major source of care for young children in many societies, and caring for grandchildren is a large part of the daily life of many older women. In India the family is the main childcare institution. Public provision for children under six runs mainly through the *anganwadi* centers of the Integrated Child Development Services, which focus on supplementary nutrition, health and pre-school education rather than full-day care, and women's labor force participation has long been low by international standards and slow to rise with education and income [@fletcher2017women_doi; @klasen2015stagnation_doi; @chatterjee2018indian]. A common presumption, in policy discussion and in the family itself, is that coresident grandparents, above all grandmothers, absorb much of the care of young children and so free mothers to work, rest or invest in other children. The presumption has empirical support elsewhere: in the United States, Europe, China and Japan the availability of grandparents is associated with, and in several quasi-experimental designs causes, higher maternal employment [@compton2014family; @posadas2013grandparents; @arpino2014grandparental; @bratti2018grandparental; @maurerfazio2011childcare; @sasaki2002causal; @ogawa1996family].

The same arrangement has a second side that matters for the economics of aging and of the family. The time that grandmothers give to grandchildren is a transfer from a generation whose own work, rest and health also matter, in a country whose older population is growing [@unfpa2023ageing; @iips2020lasi_fix]. There are also reasons to doubt that the evidence from other settings carries over. Residence after marriage is predominantly patrilocal, so the coresident grandmother is typically the mother-in-law, and the literature describes the young daughter-in-law as the junior member of a hierarchy in which her mobility and work outside the home are shaped by her husband's parents [@dyson1983kinship; @kandiyoti1988bargaining; @jayachandran2015roots; @anukriti2020curse]. Women in joint households in rural India are less likely to be employed than women in nuclear households [@dhanaraj2019family]. A three-generation household is also a larger household, with more meals to cook. Coresidence can therefore add to a mother's work as well as bring a potential substitute for her childcare. I call these the *substitution* and *constraint* channels.

Which dominates is hard to learn from existing data. Surveys of labor supply record whether a grandparent lives nearby and whether the mother works, but not what either does with the day. Surveys of grandparents record whether they look after grandchildren, but not the mother's time on the same day. The literature has therefore inferred substitution from labor-market outcomes, and the cost of care to grandmothers has rarely been measured outside high-income settings.

This paper uses India's Time Use Survey 2024 [@nso2025tus], which records a 24-hour diary, coded to the International Classification of Activities for Time-Use Statistics 2016 (ICATUS) [@un2016icatus], for every household member aged six and above. Diaries of mothers and of the grandparents who live with them are kept for the same day, and the household roster's relationship codes identify, for each married woman, the generation above her. The identification rules matter. For a woman who is a married child of the head, or the spouse of one, the generation above is the head and the head's spouse, which is the typical patrilocal arrangement. And in a household where a son and his wife live with his parents and a child under six is present, the head's wife is usually that child's grandmother, not its mother: I exclude such women from the mother sample (`r fn(n_u6_dropgm)` of `r fn(n_u6_pool)` married women aged 18 to 49 in households with a child under six) and study them as grandmothers.

The analysis has four aims. The first is to compare the time use of mothers of children under six with and without a coresident grandmother, across the whole day. The second is to ask whether three-generation households provide the same childcare more cheaply or more care in total. The third is to estimate how a young grandchild is associated with the time use of grandmothers and grandfathers, which shows the cost of care to those who give it. The fourth is to ask which grandmothers matter (by age and employment), how the association differs across household arrangements, and whether it vanishes where it should, among mothers whose youngest child is of school age.

`r iff(sub_child, paste0("A coresident grandmother is associated with ", diff_txt(k_cc), " primary childcare by the mother a day."), iff(cc_up, paste0("A coresident grandmother is associated with ", diff_txt(k_cc), " primary childcare by the mother a day, not less."), paste0("The pooled association between a coresident grandmother and the mother's primary childcare is small: ", est_se(k_cc), ".")))` The association with the mother's paid work, including travel, is `r est_se(k_emp)`. These estimates are fragile. The childcare estimate ranges from `r f1(rb_range[1])` to `r f1(rb_range[2])` minutes across the specifications in the robustness table, and subgroup estimates differ in size`r iff(emp_sign_differs, " and, for paid work, in sign", "")`. The grandmother's side is much clearer: grandmothers who live with a child under six report `r est_se(gm_cc)` of childcare a day, `r pct(gm_share_cc, 0)` of the combined childcare of mother and grandmother, and where a child under six is present they report `r diff_txt(t_cc)` primary childcare than other older women. `r iff(length(og_neg) > 0, paste0("They also report less ", and_list(og_neg), "."), "")` Summed over all household members aged 15 and above, primary childcare is `r diff_txt(k_all, "higher", "lower")` in households with a grandmother.

The paper contributes to three literatures. For the economics of grandparental childcare, it replaces inference from employment with same-day time measures for both generations, and shows that the association with mothers' time depends on the grandmother's age and employment and on the household arrangement. For research on population aging and older women, it measures directly the time that older women give to grandchildren in a patrilocal, middle-income setting and the other parts of their day from which it comes. For the study of family structure and women's work in South Asia, it documents relationship-based rules for assigning young children and grandparents in rosters that do not record parent identifiers. The estimates are conditional associations, not causal effects: living arrangements are chosen jointly with fertility, work and care, and the survey is a single cross-section.

# Background and conceptual framework

## Grandparental care and maternal employment

A large literature finds that the availability of grandparents raises mothers' labor supply. In the United States, @compton2014family show that married women who live close to their mothers or mothers-in-law have higher labor force participation, and @posadas2013grandparents find that grandparent-provided childcare raises mothers' participation. In Europe, @dimova2011downward show that downward time transfers, mainly grandchild care, raise maternal labor supply, @arpino2014grandparental find a positive effect of grandparental support in Italy, and @bratti2018grandparental exploit Italian pension reforms that raised retirement ages, and so reduced grandmothers' availability, and find lower participation among their daughters. The evidence from Asia is closer to the Indian setting because coresidence, not proximity, is the usual arrangement. @ogawa1996family and @sasaki2002causal find that coresidence with parents or parents-in-law raised Japanese married women's employment, and @maurerfazio2011childcare find a similar association in urban China, while @igel2011grandchild show that welfare states shape the form of grandparental care. For the United States, @bansak2026coresident find that living with a grandparent is positively related to employment among Asian mothers but not among white mothers.

Two features of this literature motivate the present paper. Almost all of it measures the consequence of grandparental care (maternal employment) rather than the care itself, and it comes mainly from settings in which coresidence or proximity is not tied to a strong patrilocal hierarchy. Where the grandmother is the mother-in-law and the head of the household, her presence may bring authority over the daughter-in-law's time as well as help with it.

## Older women's time, aging and intergenerational transfers

Grandparental childcare is a transfer of time between generations. Economic models distinguish altruistic from exchange motives for transfers [@cox1987motives; @altonji1997parental], and @cardia2003intergenerational show that grandparents' time is an important input into childcare. @albertini2007intergenerational document that European regimes differ in the frequency and intensity of time and money transfers across generations. Time transfers have an opportunity cost for the giver: @rupert2018grandchildren find that the arrival of grandchildren lowers grandmothers' labor supply in the United States, and @lumsdaine2015retirement that a new grandchild raises the probability that women retire. The evolutionary literature on grandmothering makes the same point from another angle, treating grandmothers' investment in grandchildren as a central and costly part of human life histories [@hawkes1998grandmothering; @sear2008keeps]. Time diaries for the older generation allow this cost to be measured directly, alongside the benefit to the mother, and allow it to be related to the grandmother's age and employment, which proxy her capacity to give care.

## Patrilocality and women's work in India

India differs from the settings above in ways that could reverse the sign of the association between coresidence and mothers' work. @dyson1983kinship argued that the kinship system of northern India, with village exogamy and patrilocal residence, limits women's autonomy, and @kandiyoti1988bargaining describes a patriarchal bargain in which young brides accept subordination in their husband's household in exchange for later authority as mothers-in-law. @anukriti2020curse show that coresident mothers-in-law restrict daughters-in-law's mobility and social networks in rural Uttar Pradesh, status concerns can lead households to withdraw women from work outside the home [@eswaran2013status], and social norms are a barrier to women's employment more broadly [@jayachandran2021social; @field2021account_fix]. @dhanaraj2019family find that women in nuclear households in rural India are more likely to work than women in joint households. These studies observe employment, autonomy or decision-making, not time.

## Measuring childcare in time diaries

Time-diary research shows that childcare is the most gendered of household tasks and that its measurement is sensitive to definitions [@sayer2004parents; @bianchi2006changing; @craig2011share_doi; @hook2006care]. Primary childcare understates the time parents are responsible for children, because supervision is often recorded as a secondary activity or not at all [@folbre2005measure; @folbre2006measuring; @kalenkoski2008quality; @craig2007contemporary]. I therefore report active and passive primary care separately, and childcare recorded as a secondary activity, because a grandmother may take over supervision while the mother keeps the care that requires her, or the reverse.

## Conceptual framework

A mother allocates her day among childcare, domestic work, paid work and leisure. A coresident grandmother changes three things. She can supply childcare, which lowers the care the mother must provide (the substitution channel); this effect should rise with the grandmother's capacity, which declines with age and ill health and falls when she works herself. She raises household size and so domestic workload, and may need care herself (a workload channel). And in a patrilocal household she may raise the cost to the household of the daughter-in-law working outside the home (a norms channel); I group the last two as the constraint channel. Four predictions follow. If substitution is present, mothers' childcare is lower with a grandmother, more so for passive minding than for active care. Whether released time reaches paid work depends on the constraint channel, and if it is strong, released time shows up in domestic work or leisure. The grandmother's own time should show the other side, with more childcare and less of something else when a young grandchild is present. And substitution should be larger with grandmothers who have more capacity (younger, not employed) and concentrated where the youngest child is under six. The framework does not model the choice of living arrangement, the main threat to interpretation discussed below.

# Data and methods

## The Time Use Survey 2024

The Time Use Survey (TUS) 2024 was conducted by the National Statistics Office, Ministry of Statistics and Programme Implementation, between January and December 2024 [@nso2025tus]. It covers a nationally representative sample of households in rural and urban India, drawn in a stratified multi-stage design with First Stage Units (villages and urban blocks) as primary sampling units. Every member aged six and above reports a 24-hour diary for the day before the interview, from 4 a.m. to 4 a.m., in time slots that can contain several activities. Each activity is coded to ICATUS 2016 and flagged as major or minor (secondary). I use every activity record: `r fn(V$n_rows)` records for `r fn(V$n_diarists)` diarists in `r fn(V$n_households)` households and `r fn(V$n_fsu)` First Stage Units. Minutes of major activities are summed to the person-day, and all but `r nw(V$n_diaries_not1440)` of the `r fn(V$n_diarists)` diaries sum to exactly 1,440 minutes. `r iff(V$n_third_gender > 0, paste0("I exclude ", nw(V$n_third_gender), " persons recorded as third gender from the analyses because the sample is too small for separate estimates; they remain in household composition. "), "")`Weights are the survey multipliers, and standard errors are clustered on the First Stage Unit [@abadie2023cluster_doi; @solon2015weighting]. The survey construction checks and the sample construction are in Online Resource 1.

## Identifying mothers, children and grandparents

Children under six do not keep diaries but are listed on the household roster, so the number of under-six members is a direct count of roster members aged under six (the file contains members of all ages). `r iff(!is.na(share_roster_hh), paste0("As a check, the roster count of household members equals the household size recorded in the household file for ", pct(share_roster_hh, 1), " of households. "), "")`The roster does not record the identifier of each child's mother. The candidate mothers are married women aged 18 to 49 whose relationship to the head is head or spouse of head (head level), or married child or spouse of a married child (junior level). Women with other relationships, such as a brother's wife, are excluded because the roster does not identify the generation above them. In a household in which a married child of the head lives with a spouse, a child under six is far more likely to be the junior couple's child, that is, the head's grandchild, than a late-born child of the head. I therefore exclude from the mother sample head-level women who live with a junior-level married woman aged 15 to 49 (`r fn(n_u6_dropgm)` women), and study them as grandmothers. The analysis sample consists of the `r fn(n_my)` remaining women in households with at least one child under six. Of these, `r pct(share_jun, 0)` are at junior level, and among junior-level mothers `r pct(share_dil, 0)` are daughters-in-law of the head. The husband is linked to `r pct(share_hus, 0)` of mothers through the roster; I keep mothers whose husbands live elsewhere in the sample, with an explicit indicator.

For a head-level mother, the generation above her consists of members coded as father, mother, father-in-law or mother-in-law of the head. For a junior-level mother it consists of the head and the head's spouse aged 40 or above. A coresident grandmother is at least one woman in this generation, and a coresident grandfather at least one man. Because each mother is matched to the specific members of the generation above her, a grandmother is never the mother herself (`r nw(n_self_links)` self-links). By this definition `r pct(share_gm, 0)` of mothers of children under six live with a grandmother and `r pct(share_gf, 0)` with a grandfather; `r pct(share_gfo, 1)` live with a grandfather but no grandmother. Among mothers with a coresident grandmother, `r pct(share_jun_gm, 0)` are at junior level, so most three-generation households are of the patrilocal type in which the young family lives in the older generation's household. The median age of the youngest coresident grandmother is `r f0(gm_age_med)` years, `r pct(share_gm_young, 0)` of grandmothers are under 60, and `r pct(share_gm_work, 0)` report employment as their usual principal activity status.

## Time outcomes

Childcare is ICATUS 411 to 419 plus accompanying own children (442). Active care (411 to 415) covers physical care, medical care, teaching, talking and reading, and playing; passive care (416) is minding children. I also measure childcare recorded as a secondary activity, unpaid domestic services (division three) and within it food and meals (311 to 319), care of dependent adults (421 to 429 and 443), employment including related travel (division one), free time (divisions seven and eight) and sleep (911 to 919). Employment status is the usual principal activity status.



Table \ref{tab:desc} compares the raw time use of mothers with and without a coresident grandmother. Mothers without a grandmother report `r est_se(mo_cc0)` of primary childcare a day and mothers with one `r est_se(mo_cc1)`. The raw comparison mixes the grandmother's presence with everything that differs between joint and nuclear households, which motivates the regression approach.

```{r tab-desc}
dt <- rbind(means_table(MY, outs, "gp_lab", unname(out_lab[outs])),
            means_table(MY, "employed", "gp_lab", unname(out_lab["employed"]), digits = 3))
tab(dt, caption = paste0("Mothers of children under six: minutes per day by grandmother coresidence", syn_note()),
    label = "desc", align = c("l", "r", "r"), escape = FALSE,
    notes = "Married women aged 18--49 at head or junior level in households with a child under six, excluding head-level women who live with a junior married woman of childbearing age. Survey-weighted means; FSU-clustered standard errors in parentheses. Employed is a share (three decimals).")
```

## Empirical strategy

For mother $i$ in household $h$, state $s$ and diary day $d$, I estimate

\begin{equation}\label{eq:main} y_{ih} = \beta\, \textit{GM}_{h} + X_{ih}'\gamma + \mu_s + \tau_d + \varepsilon_{ih}, \end{equation}

where $y_{ih}$ is a time outcome in minutes per day (or employment status) and $\textit{GM}_h$ indicates a coresident grandmother. $X_{ih}$ includes the mother's age band and education, the husband's education and usual employment (with a separate category for mothers without a linked husband), the household's per-capita consumption quintile, urban residence, the number of children under six and aged six to 14, the number of the mother's own children aged six to 17, caste group, religion, whether any member needs special care, and whether the diary was reported by a proxy. State fixed effects absorb regional kinship systems and labor markets, and day-of-week fixed effects absorb the weekly cycle. I do not control for household size in the main specification, because a grandmother raises it mechanically and the workload that comes with a larger household is part of the constraint channel; a robustness check adds it. I report 95% confidence intervals (CI) based on the normal approximation, not significance tests. In the text, an interval attached to a difference refers to the signed coefficient, with households without a grandmother as the reference.

The main threat to interpretation is selection into coresidence. Three-generation households differ from nuclear ones in wealth, caste, region and norms, and coresidence can respond to care needs: a grandmother may move in because a grandchild is born, or because she needs care herself. I read $\beta$ as a conditional association and assess it in four ways. First, I compare arrangements selected for different reasons. Junior-level mothers live in the older generation's household, the default patrilocal arrangement; head-level mothers whose parents or in-laws live with them have taken the older generation in, which is more often driven by the grandparents' need for support. Most junior-level mothers live with a grandmother (`r fn(n_jun_nogm)` do not, against `r fn(n_jun_gm)` who do), so the grandmother indicator is closely tied to the household arrangement, and where either cell has fewer than `r MIN_CELL` mothers I do not report the estimate. Second, I examine gradients that the substitution channel predicts but selection on fixed household traits does not obviously predict, by the grandmother's age, employment and sex. Third, I estimate the specification for mothers whose youngest child is aged six to 14 and who have no child under six in the household, among whom substitution of childcare should be weaker. Fourth, I report the bias-adjusted coefficient of @oster2019unobservable [see also @altonji2005selection].

The older generation's time is estimated on a separate sample of `r fn(n_ogw)` women and `r fn(n_ogm)` men aged 45 to 80 in the generation above a married woman of childbearing age. I regress the same outcomes on an indicator for a child under six in the household, with controls for age band, education, marital status, urban residence, consumption quintile, children aged six to 14, caste, religion, special care needs and proxy reporting, and state and day fixed effects. The comparison is between older-generation members whose grandchildren are young and those whose grandchildren are older or not yet born, which depends on the timing of the junior couple's fertility rather than on the decision to coreside.

## Ethics, data availability and the use of AI tools

The analysis uses anonymized unit-level data released by the National Statistics Office and involved no contact with respondents; no ethical review was required. The microdata are available from the Ministry's microdata portal subject to its terms of use; analysis code will be made available on acceptance. AI tools (Claude (Anthropic) and other AI assistants) were used to help write and check analysis code, to check references and to draft text. The author reviewed and verified all code, results, references and text and takes full responsibility for the content.

# Results

## Mothers' time



Table \ref{tab:main} reports the main estimates. A coresident grandmother is associated with `r diff_txt(k_cc)` primary childcare by the mother a day. Relative to the mean of mothers without a grandmother, `r f1(base_cc)` minutes, the point estimate is `r pct(abs(k_cc$est) / base_cc, 0)` of the baseline. `r iff(ci_incl0(k_cc), paste0("The interval includes zero: the data are compatible with a reduction of up to ", pct(abs(min(k_cc$est - 1.96 * k_cc$se, 0)) / base_cc, 0), " of the baseline and with no change."), "")` The split by type of care shows `r est_se(k_act)` for active care and `r est_se(k_pas)` for passive minding. `r iff(pas_only, "The difference is concentrated in passive minding, the form of care most easily shared, while mothers retain active care, as the first prediction of the framework implies.", iff(act_too, "Grandmothers' presence is associated with less active care by mothers as well, not only less minding, so the difference extends to tasks that require more of the carer.", iff(ci_incl0(k_act) && ci_incl0(k_pas), "The intervals for both components include zero.", "")))` `r iff(is_neg(k_sec), paste0("Mothers with a coresident grandmother also record less childcare as a secondary activity (", est_se(k_sec), "), so the lower supervision is not confined to primary care."), paste0("Childcare recorded as a secondary activity differs by ", est_se(k_sec), "."))`

```{r tab-main}
rows <- c(outs, "employed")
rt <- data.frame(Outcome = unname(out_lab[rows]),
                 Mean = sapply(rows, function(y) if (y == "employed") f3(wmean(MY[gm_any == 0][[y]], MY[gm_any == 0]$weight)) else f1(wmean(MY[gm_any == 0][[y]], MY[gm_any == 0]$weight))),
                 Coefficient = sapply(rows, function(y) cell(coef_of(m_gm[[y]], "gm_any"), if (y == "employed") 3 else 2)),
                 `95 percent CI` = sapply(rows, function(y) ci_cell(coef_of(m_gm[[y]], "gm_any"), if (y == "employed") 3 else 2)),
                 N = sapply(rows, function(y) if (is.null(m_gm[[y]])) "--" else fn(nobs(m_gm[[y]]))),
                 check.names = FALSE)
tab(rt, caption = paste0("Coresident grandmother and mothers' time use", syn_note()), label = "main",
    align = c("l", "r", "r", "r", "r"), escape = FALSE,
    notes = "Each row is a separate regression of the outcome (minutes per day, or a 0/1 indicator for usual employment) on an indicator for a coresident grandmother and the full control set, with state and day-of-week fixed effects. Mean: outcome mean for mothers without a coresident grandmother. Survey-weighted; FSU-clustered standard errors; 95 percent confidence intervals use the normal approximation.")
```

The remaining rows show where the mother's day goes. Unpaid domestic work differs by `r est_se(k_dom)``r iff(is_pos(k_food) && !is_pos(k_dom), paste0(", but time on food and meals, the largest domestic task and the one most directly raised by household size, is higher by ", est_se(k_food), ", an interval that excludes zero"), paste0(", of which food and meals ", est_se(k_food)))`. Care of dependent adults differs by `r est_se(k_adult)`. Employment including travel differs by `r est_se(k_emp)`, and the probability that the mother's usual status is employed is `r diff_pp(k_lfp)`. `r iff(emp_up || lfp_up, "Some of any time released reaches paid work.", iff(emp_down || is_neg(k_lfp), "Neither measure shows more paid work with a grandmother present, and the employment-rate estimate points to a small reduction, a pattern that is consistent with the constraint channel in patrilocal households although these data do not isolate it.", "Neither measure shows more paid work with a grandmother present."))` Free time is `r diff_txt(k_ft, "higher", "lower")` and sleep `r diff_txt(k_sleep, "higher", "lower")`. `r iff(!ci_incl0(k_ft) && !ci_incl0(k_sleep) && max(abs(c(k_ft$est, k_sleep$est))) < 10, "Both intervals exclude zero, but the differences amount to a few minutes in a day of 1,440.", "These are small differences relative to the day.")`

`r iff(!emp_up && !lfp_up && !sub_child, "Taken together, the pooled estimates show small differences in mothers' time, no sign that a grandmother's presence raises mothers' paid work, and an association with childcare whose interval includes zero. They do not show that grandmothers relieve mothers of care, and, as the robustness checks and subgroup results below show, they hide differences by grandmother and by household arrangement.", iff(sub_child && !emp_up && !lfp_up, "Taken together, the pattern is consistent with the second prediction when the constraint channel is strong: grandmothers' presence is associated with less childcare by mothers but not with more employment. The data do not identify the constraint itself.", iff(emp_up || lfp_up, "Taken together, the results suggest that coresident grandmothers relax the time constraint of mothers enough to raise their paid work.", "")))`

## Who provides childcare in three-generation households



Table \ref{tab:who} (and Fig. \ref{fig:fig-providers} in Online Resource 1) decompose the childcare provided by household members. In households with a grandmother, grandmothers provide `r est_se(gm_cc)` of childcare a day. They also report `r est_se(gm_dom)` of domestic work and `r est_se(gm_empm)` of employment, which shows what else their day contains. Because a grandmother adds a carer, the relevant comparison is total childcare, conditional on the number of children of each age. Summed over all members aged 15 and above, childcare is `r diff_txt(k_all, "higher", "lower")` in households with a grandmother. `r iff(hh_more, "Children in three-generation households thus receive more adult childcare time, not the same care more cheaply. Part of the difference may reflect two adults recording care of the same child at the same time, and part the care of several grandchildren at once; the diary does not identify the recipient.", iff(hh_less, "Children in three-generation households receive less adult childcare time in total, which would be the case if coresidence brings competing demands on the adults.", "The interval for total adult childcare includes zero."))` Husbands' childcare, for those linked, differs by `r est_se(k_fa)` with a grandmother's presence. `r iff(is_neg(k_fa), "Grandmothers' care therefore appears to replace part of fathers' contribution, which is modest, as well as adding to the household's total.", "")`

```{r tab-who}
who_y <- c("care_child", "father_cc", "gm_care_child", "gf_care_child", "others_cc", "hh_cc_all")
who_l <- c("Mother", "Husband (if linked)", "Grandmother(s)", "Grandfather(s)",
           "Other members aged 15+", "All members aged 15+")
wt <- means_table(MY, who_y, "gp_lab", who_l)
tab(wt, caption = paste0("Childcare minutes per day by provider, households with a child under six", syn_note()),
    label = "who", align = c("l", "r", "r"),
    notes = "Unit: mothers in the analysis sample. Minutes of primary childcare of each household member, survey-weighted means with FSU-clustered standard errors; 95 percent confidence intervals use the normal approximation. Other members include husbands who are not linked through the roster. All members is the household total and includes care given to other children in the household.")
```

## The older generation's time



Table \ref{tab:og} (and Fig. \ref{fig:fig-og} in Online Resource 1) turns to the providers of care. Among older-generation women, a child under six in the household is associated with `r diff_txt(t_cc)` primary childcare a day, against a mean of `r f1(wmean(OGW[young_gc == 0]$care_child, OGW[young_gc == 0]$weight))` minutes for women without a young grandchild. `r iff(gm_cost_cc, "On the care side the third prediction of the framework holds: grandmothers report more childcare when a young grandchild is present.", "Grandmothers do not report more childcare when a young grandchild is present, which casts doubt on the substitution channel itself.")` The associations with grandmothers' domestic work (`r est_se(t_dom)`), paid work (`r est_se(t_emp)`), employment status (`r diff_pp(t_lfp)`), free time (`r est_se(t_ft)`) and sleep (`r est_se(t_sleep)`) indicate where that time comes from. `r iff(length(og_neg) > 0, paste0("Grandmothers with a young grandchild report less ", and_list(og_neg), ", with confidence intervals that exclude zero, so the care they provide has a cost in their own time. ", iff(any(grepl("free time", og_neg)) && abs(t_ft$est) == max(abs(c(t_dom$est, t_ft$est, t_sleep$est))), paste0("The fall in free time is the largest, at ", pct(abs(t_ft$est) / wmean(OGW[young_gc == 0]$free_time, OGW[young_gc == 0]$weight), 0), " of the mean for women without a young grandchild."), "")), "No component is clearly lower, so the diaries do not reveal a single activity from which the extra childcare is drawn.")` `r iff(is_neg(t_emp) || is_neg(t_lfp), "Part of the cost therefore falls on their own earnings, as in the evidence for the United States [@rupert2018grandchildren].", paste0("Their paid work does not fall", iff(length(og_neg) > 0, paste0(", so in this sample the cost falls on ", and_list(og_neg), " rather than on earnings"), ""), "."))`

```{r tab-og}
og_lab <- c(care_child = "Childcare (primary)", care_child_active = "\\quad Active childcare",
            care_child_passive = "\\quad Passive childcare (minding)", unpaid_domestic = "Unpaid domestic work",
            employment = "Employment (incl. travel)", employed = "Employed (usual status, share)",
            free_time = "Free time", sleep = "Sleep")
ot <- data.frame(Outcome = unname(og_lab[og_outs]),
                 `Mean, women` = sapply(og_outs, function(y) (if (y == "employed") f3 else f1)(wmean(OGW[young_gc == 0][[y]], OGW[young_gc == 0]$weight))),
                 Grandmothers = sapply(og_outs, function(y) cse(T_gm[[y]], if (y == "employed") 3 else 2)),
                 Grandfathers = sapply(og_outs, function(y) cse(T_gf[[y]], if (y == "employed") 3 else 2)),
                 Difference = sapply(og_outs, function(y) cse(T_dd[[y]], if (y == "employed") 3 else 2)),
                 check.names = FALSE)
tab(ot, caption = paste0("The older generation: time use and a child under six in the household", syn_note()),
    label = "og", align = c("l", "r", "r", "r", "r"), escape = FALSE,
    notes = paste0("Members aged 45--80 in the generation above a married woman of childbearing age (", fn(n_ogw), " women, ", fn(n_ogm), " men). Estimate [95 percent confidence interval] for an indicator for a child under six in the household, separately for women and men; Difference: women minus men, with a standard error that ignores the covariance of the two estimates (conservative, since grandmothers and grandfathers often share a household). Mean: women without a child under six. Controls: age band, education, marital status, urban, consumption quintile, children 6--14, caste, religion, special care need, proxy report; state and day fixed effects. FSU-clustered standard errors; 95 percent confidence intervals use the normal approximation."))
```

For older-generation men, the corresponding childcare association is `r est_se(tf_cc)`, and the women-minus-men difference is `r est_se(td_cc)`. `r iff(gf_less, "The care response of the older generation falls overwhelmingly on grandmothers, mirroring the gender division of care in the middle generation.", iff(is_sig(td_cc), "Grandfathers' childcare responds more than grandmothers' on this measure.", "The interval for the difference between grandmothers and grandfathers includes zero."))` Paid work of older men differs by `r est_se(tf_emp)`.`r iff(is_pos(tf_emp) && !is_pos(t_emp), " It is higher for older men but not clearly for older women, so the adjustment to a young grandchild differs by gender beyond the amount of care.", "")`

## Which grandmothers matter



Table \ref{tab:gptype} examines the fourth prediction. Grandmother age proxies for health and stamina, which the survey does not measure directly. Relative to mothers without a grandmother, the coefficient on mothers' childcare is `r est_se(A$young$cc)` for a grandmother under 60 and `r est_se(A$old$cc)` for a grandmother aged 60 or older; the difference is `r est_se(A$dage$cc)`. `r iff(age_grad && isTRUE(A$dage$cc$est < 0), "Younger grandmothers are associated with a larger reduction in mothers' childcare, as the capacity part of the substitution channel predicts.", iff(age_grad, "The reduction in mothers' childcare is concentrated where the grandmother is 60 or older, and the interval for the difference excludes zero. This runs against a simple capacity story in which younger grandmothers are fitter, but it is consistent with older grandmothers being less likely to be in paid work and so more available at home.", "The interval for the difference by grandmother age includes zero."))`

```{r tab-who-gp}
gr <- data.frame(
  Comparison = c("Grandmother under 60", "Grandmother 60 or older", "\\quad Difference (under 60 minus 60+)",
                 "Grandmother not employed", "Grandmother employed", "\\quad Difference (not employed minus employed)",
                 "Grandmother only", "Grandfather only", "Both grandparents",
                 "\\quad Difference (grandmother only minus grandfather only)"),
  Childcare = c(cse(A$young$cc), cse(A$old$cc), cse(A$dage$cc), cse(A$nowork$cc), cse(A$work$cc), cse(A$dwork$cc),
                cse(A$gmo$cc), cse(A$gfo$cc), cse(A$both$cc), cse(A$dsex$cc)),
  Employment = c(cse(A$young$emp), cse(A$old$emp), cse(A$dage$emp), cse(A$nowork$emp), cse(A$work$emp), cse(A$dwork$emp),
                 cse(A$gmo$emp), cse(A$gfo$emp), cse(A$both$emp), cse(A$dsex$emp)),
  check.names = FALSE)
tab(gr, caption = paste0("Mothers' childcare and employment minutes by type of coresident grandparent", syn_note()),
    label = "gptype", align = c("l", "r", "r"), escape = FALSE,
    notes = "Each block is one regression per outcome with mutually exclusive indicators; the omitted group is mothers with no coresident grandmother (first two blocks) or no coresident grandparent (third block). Age is that of the youngest coresident grandmother; employment is usual principal activity status. Controls as in the main specification. Estimate [95 percent confidence interval]; FSU-clustered.")
```

An employed grandmother has less time to give. The coefficient is `r est_se(A$nowork$cc)` for a grandmother who is not employed and `r est_se(A$work$cc)` for one who is, a difference of `r est_se(A$dwork$cc)`. `r iff(work_grad && isTRUE(A$dwork$cc$est < 0), "Substitution is concentrated among grandmothers who are not in paid work; with an employed grandmother mothers' childcare is not lower.", iff(work_grad, "Contrary to the capacity prediction, the association is stronger with employed grandmothers.", "The interval for the difference by grandmother's employment includes zero."))` Grandmothers' age, employment and household position are related, and employment is itself a choice made jointly with the care they provide, so these comparisons are descriptive.

The last block separates grandmothers from grandfathers. The coefficient on mothers' childcare is `r est_se(A$gmo$cc)` for a grandmother without a grandfather, `r est_se(A$gfo$cc)` for a grandfather without a grandmother, and `r est_se(A$both$cc)` for both together. `r iff(sex_grad && isTRUE(A$dsex$cc$est < 0), "The association is more negative for grandmothers than for grandfathers, with an interval for the difference that excludes zero.", iff(sex_grad, "The association is more negative for grandfathers, which runs against the gendered-norm prediction.", "The interval for the difference between grandmothers and grandfathers includes zero; households with only a grandfather are few, so this comparison is imprecise."))` Mothers' paid work is `r diff_txt(A$gmo$emp, "higher", "lower")` with a grandmother only and `r diff_txt(A$both$emp, "higher", "lower")` with both grandparents`r iff(emp_sign_differs, ", so the pooled employment estimate averages associations of different sign", "")`. `r iff(age_grad || work_grad || sex_grad, "These gradients are consistent with substitution where the older generation has time to give, which a fixed household trait would not obviously predict, but they do not rule out selection.", "Because none of these gradients is distinguishable from zero, they do not help to separate substitution from selection.")`

## Differences by household arrangement



Table \ref{tab:het} reports the estimates by subsample. For head-level mothers, whose parents or in-laws live in their household, the childcare association is `r hx(H$head)` and the employment association `r hx(H_emp$head)`. `r iff(jun_estimable, paste0("For junior-level mothers, who live in their in-laws' or parents' household, the childcare association is ", hx(H$jun), " and the employment association ", hx(H_emp$jun), ", estimated from only ", fn(n_jun_nogm), " junior-level mothers without a grandmother. The two arrangements are selected for different reasons, the first more often by the grandparents' need for support and the second by the patrilocal norm, and ", iff(is_sig(ddiff(H$head, H$jun)), "the estimates differ.", "the estimates are too imprecise to distinguish them.")), paste0("For junior-level mothers, who live in the older generation's household, the estimate is not reported: only ", fn(n_jun_nogm), " of the ", fn(n_jun_nogm + n_jun_gm), " junior-level mothers live without a coresident grandmother, too few to separate her presence from the arrangement itself."))` `r iff(!jun_estimable, "The head-level estimate therefore describes mothers whose parents or in-laws have joined their household, and it should not be generalized to the junior arrangement.", "")` Because most junior-level mothers live with a grandmother, the pooled grandmother indicator partly captures the difference between the two arrangements. With a control for the mother's generation the estimate is `r est_se(RB[[8]])` (see the robustness checks below), compared with `r est_se(k_cc)` in the pooled specification.

```{r tab-het}
hl <- c(head = "Head-level mother (grandparents live in her household)",
        jun = "Junior-level mother (lives in the older generation's household)",
        urb = "Urban", rur = "Rural", elo = "Mother below secondary education",
        ehi = "Mother secondary education or above", one = "One child under six", two = "Two or more children under six")
hcell <- function(k) if (!isTRUE(k$ok)) "not estimable" else cse(k)
ht <- data.frame(Subsample = unname(hl[names(splits)]),
                 Childcare = sapply(names(splits), function(s) hcell(H[[s]])),
                 Employment = sapply(names(splits), function(s) hcell(H_emp[[s]])),
                 N = sapply(names(splits), function(s) fn(nrow(splits[[s]]))), check.names = FALSE)
tab(ht, caption = paste0("Heterogeneity: grandmother coresidence and mothers' childcare and employment minutes", syn_note()),
    label = "het", align = c("l", "r", "r", "r"),
    notes = paste0("Main specification, estimated separately by subsample. Estimate [95 percent confidence interval] for the grandmother indicator. Not estimable: fewer than ", MIN_CELL, " mothers with or without a coresident grandmother in the subsample."))
```

Across urban and rural households the childcare associations are `r hx(H$urb)` and `r hx(H$rur)`. By the mother's education they are `r hx(H$elo)` below secondary and `r hx(H$ehi)` at secondary or above. More educated mothers have better labor-market options, so if grandmothers' help reaches paid work anywhere it should be among them; the corresponding employment associations are `r hx(H_emp$elo)` and `r hx(H_emp$ehi)`, and by urban and rural residence `r hx(H_emp$urb)` and `r hx(H_emp$rur)`. With one child under six the childcare association is `r hx(H$one)`, and with two or more `r hx(H$two)`. `r iff(isTRUE(H_emp$urb$ok) && isTRUE(H_emp$rur$ok) && sign(H_emp$urb$est) != sign(H_emp$rur$est), "The employment associations differ in sign between urban and rural mothers, which again shows that the pooled employment estimate should not be read as evidence of no association.", "")`

## A placebo: mothers of school-age children



If grandmothers substitute for the care of young children, the association with mothers' childcare should be weaker where the youngest child is of school age and needs less supervision. If instead the main estimate reflects fixed differences between joint and nuclear households, it should be similar for both groups of mothers. Table \ref{tab:placebo} reports the comparison for `r fn(n_mp)` mothers whose youngest identified own child is aged six to 14 and who have no child under six in the household. The childcare association is `r est_se(k_pl)` in this group, against `r est_se(k_cc)` in the analysis sample, and the difference between the two is `r est_se(k_dd)`. `r iff(sub_child && pl_null && is_neg(k_dd), "The association with childcare is confined to mothers of young children, as substitution implies and fixed-trait selection does not.", iff(sub_child && !is_neg(k_dd), "The association is not weaker for mothers of school-age children, which leaves room for selection on household traits to explain part of the main estimate.", iff(!sub_child, "Because the main childcare estimate is itself small, the childcare comparison is not informative on its own.", "")))` The placebo is not fully clean. The association with domestic work, which the constraint channel predicts should not depend on the child's age, is `r est_se(PL$unpaid_domestic$pl)` in the placebo group and `r est_se(PL$unpaid_domestic$u6)` in the analysis sample`r iff(is_pos(PL$unpaid_domestic$pl), ", so a grandmother's presence is associated with more domestic work among mothers of school-age children, for whom the substitution channel should be weak. This pattern is consistent with a workload effect of larger households and with selection, and it means the placebo cannot rule out that part of the main estimates reflects household traits", "")`.

```{r tab-placebo}
plab <- c(care_child = "Childcare (primary)", care_child_active = "\\quad Active childcare",
          care_child_passive = "\\quad Passive childcare (minding)", unpaid_domestic = "Unpaid domestic work",
          employment = "Employment (incl. travel)")
pt <- data.frame(Outcome = unname(plab[pl_outs]),
                 `Child under six` = sapply(pl_outs, function(y) cse(PL[[y]]$u6)),
                 `Youngest child 6--14` = sapply(pl_outs, function(y) cse(PL[[y]]$pl)),
                 Difference = sapply(pl_outs, function(y) cse(PL[[y]]$dd)), check.names = FALSE)
tab(pt, caption = paste0("Placebo: grandmother coresidence for mothers whose youngest child is aged 6 to 14", syn_note()),
    label = "placebo", align = c("l", "r", "r", "r"), escape = FALSE,
    notes = paste0("Estimate [95 percent confidence interval] for the grandmother indicator. Column 1: analysis sample (", fn(n_my), " mothers). Column 2: mothers defined in the same way with no child under six in the household and an identified youngest own child aged 6 to 14 (", fn(n_mp), " mothers). Difference: column 1 minus column 2, with a standard error that ignores the covariance of the two estimates. Controls as in the main specification."))
```

## Robustness



Table \ref{tab:robust} collects robustness checks for the childcare estimate. Restricting to households with a single married woman aged 18 to 49, where the child under six is most likely hers, gives `r est_se(RB[[2]])`. Restricting to head-level mothers gives `r est_se(RB[[3]])`. Requiring a linked husband gives `r est_se(RB[[4]])`, and dropping proxy-reported diaries gives `r est_se(RB[[5]])`. Adding the number of other adult women gives `r est_se(RB[[6]])`; adding household size gives `r est_se(RB[[7]])`; and adding an indicator for the mother's generation gives `r est_se(RB[[8]])`. The unweighted estimate is `r est_se(RB[[9]])`, and broadening the treatment to any grandparent gives `r est_se(RB[[10]])`. On the extensive margin, a grandmother is associated with a `r diff_pp(k_any_cc)` probability that the mother reports any primary childcare. `r iff(rb_sign_stable, paste0("All estimates have the same sign, ranging from ", f1(rb_range[1]), " to ", f1(rb_range[2]), " minutes."), paste0("The estimates range from ", f1(rb_range[1]), " to ", f1(rb_range[2]), " minutes and do not all share a sign, so the main childcare estimate should be read as fragile: its sign and size depend on whether household size, the mother's generation or the household arrangement is held constant."))` The bias-adjusted coefficient of @oster2019unobservable, which assumes that unobservables are as important as observables and that the maximum attainable $R^2$ is 1.3 times that of the full model, is `r f2(ob)` for childcare and `r f2(obe)` for employment. `r iff(oster_same_sign && sub_child, "The childcare estimate keeps its sign under this adjustment.", iff(sub_child, "Under this adjustment the childcare estimate changes sign, so a moderate degree of selection on unobservables could account for it.", ""))`

```{r robust}
rb <- data.frame(Check = c(names(RB), "Extensive margin: any primary childcare (share)",
                           "Oster bias-adjusted, childcare (delta = 1, Rmax = 1.3 R)",
                           "Oster bias-adjusted, employment (delta = 1, Rmax = 1.3 R)"),
                 Estimate = c(vapply(RB, cell, character(1)), cell(k_any_cc, 3), f2(ob), f2(obe)),
                 `95 percent CI` = c(vapply(RB, ci_cell, character(1)), ci_cell(k_any_cc, 3), "", ""),
                 check.names = FALSE)
tab(rb, caption = paste0("Robustness: mothers' primary childcare minutes", syn_note()), label = "robust",
    align = c("l", "r", "r"),
    notes = "Coefficient on the grandmother indicator (or any grandparent) in the main specification, unless stated. The extensive-margin row is a linear probability model. The Oster rows use the short regression without controls or fixed effects on the same sample.")
```

# Discussion and conclusion

## Interpretation

`r iff(!sub_child && !(emp_up || lfp_up), paste0("The pooled association between a coresident grandmother and a mother's primary childcare is small, with a 95% CI of ", cilo(k_cc), " to ", cihi(k_cc), " minutes a day, and the interval for paid work, ", cilo(k_emp), " to ", cihi(k_emp), " minutes, also includes zero. These intervals describe one specification. The childcare estimate changes size and sign when the comparison changes (Table \\ref{tab:robust}), and it differs by grandmother and by household arrangement (Tables \\ref{tab:gptype} and \\ref{tab:het}). The pooled estimate is therefore best read as an average over different associations, not as evidence that grandmothers' care has no effect on mothers' time."), "")`

The clearest evidence concerns grandmothers. Where a child under six is present, grandmothers report much more childcare than other older women`r iff(length(og_neg) > 0, paste0(", and less ", and_list(og_neg)), "")``r iff(!is_neg(t_emp) && !is_neg(t_lfp), ", while their paid work does not fall", "")`. `r iff(length(og_neg) > 0, paste0("Grandmothering in this setting is a substantial transfer of time from older women, and its cost falls on ", and_list(og_neg), "."), "Grandmothering in this setting is a substantial transfer of time from older women.")` `r iff(gm_cost_cc && hh_more, "Children in three-generation households also receive more adult care in total, so the grandmother's care adds to what children receive.", "")`

For mothers, three readings are consistent with the pattern, and the evidence allows only a partial ranking. The first is substitution where the grandmother has time. `r iff(cap_pattern, paste0("Mothers' childcare is lower where the grandmother is 60 or older and not in paid work and is not lower where she is younger or employed", iff(is_neg(H$head), ", and among head-level mothers the reduction is larger", ""), "."), "The gradients by the grandmother's age and employment (Table \\ref{tab:gptype}) are the evidence on this reading, and they are not uniformly in the predicted direction.")` The second is the constraint channel: a larger household and a senior woman's authority raise the mother's domestic load and the wedge on work outside the home, so any childcare time released is absorbed`r iff(is_pos(k_food), ", which fits the higher time on food and meals", "")`. The third is selection: mothers who choose, or are placed in, three-generation households differ in ways that also shape their time. Gradients by the grandmother's characteristics are harder to attribute to fixed household traits, but selection remains open: the pooled estimate is sensitive to the specification`r iff(is_pos(PL$unpaid_domestic$pl), ", and the placebo for domestic work is not clean", "")`. `r iff(is_neg(k_fa), "Fathers' childcare is also lower with a grandmother present, so part of grandmothers' care appears to replace fathers' contribution rather than mothers'.", "")`

Studies in the United States, Europe, Japan and China find that grandparents raise maternal employment [@compton2014family; @dimova2011downward; @bratti2018grandparental; @sasaki2002causal; @maurerfazio2011childcare]. `r iff(!emp_up && !lfp_up, paste0("The pooled estimates here show no such association in India, although grandmothers provide ", pct(gm_share_cc, 0), " of the combined childcare of the two women", iff(emp_sign_differs, ", and the subgroup estimates for paid work differ in sign", ""), ". The contrast is consistent with the view that the binding constraint on young Indian mothers' employment is not, or not only, the availability of childcare, and with the evidence that household structure and norms restrict married women's work in India [@dhanaraj2019family; @anukriti2020curse; @jayachandran2021social], although these data cannot establish it."), "The estimates here show a positive association with mothers' paid work, in line with the studies above.")` The Norwegian finding that formal childcare mainly crowded out informal care [@havnes2011money] is a useful parallel: when one form of care replaces another, the effect on mothers' work depends on what else constrains it.

## Implications for research and policy

Policy on childcare and policy on older people's wellbeing are usually considered separately. These results suggest that they interact. Family care is not free: it is provided by older women whose own free time and sleep fall when a young grandchild is present. As India's population ages [@unfpa2023ageing; @iips2020lasi_fix], the supply of grandmother care will depend on older women's health, employment and household position, and the implicit cost to them belongs in any assessment of how families, and public provision, share the care of young children. Expanding formal childcare may matter for mothers in extended households as well as in nuclear ones, although its effect will depend on whether the constraints of the extended household also bind on the use of formal care. All of these statements rest on conditional associations from one cross-section and should be treated with caution.

## Limitations

The limitations are those of a single cross-section of diaries. Living arrangements are chosen, and the gradients, the placebo, the comparison of arrangements and the coefficient-stability bounds narrow but do not eliminate the scope for selection. Most junior-level mothers live with a grandmother, so the grandmother indicator is entangled with the household arrangement, and a design that compares mothers within the same arrangement would be preferable. The survey offers no credible instrument for coresidence. One diary day per person measures a day, not a routine [@frazis2012think_fix], which adds noise to individual outcomes but does not bias population means. Children under six are counted from the roster and assigned to a mother by a generational rule; the estimate that restricts to households with a single married woman of childbearing age is `r est_se(RB[[2]])`, but misassignment in households with several junior couples cannot be ruled out. The roster code for parents of the head does not distinguish the head's own parents from the spouse's parents, so for head-level mothers the maternal and paternal grandmother cannot be separated. Grandmother age proxies for health only imperfectly. Finally, the survey does not record which child a care episode is for, so in households with several young children the grandmother's recorded care may serve children other than the mother's. Future rounds that record the recipient of care, and surveys that follow the same families over the birth of a grandchild, would allow sharper tests.

## Conclusion

Diaries for every member of the household make it possible to measure directly what grandmothers and mothers do with the day in three-generation households. Identifying the generation above each mother correctly matters, because in patrilocal households the young mother lives in her parents-in-law's household and, unless the roster is read carefully, the head's wife would be counted as a mother rather than as the grandmother she is. With that identification, `r iff(!sub_child && !emp_up && !lfp_up, "the pooled association between a coresident grandmother and mothers' childcare or paid work is small and not robust, while grandmothers' own childcare is substantial and is associated with less domestic work, free time and sleep for them", "coresident grandmothers are associated with different amounts of mothers' childcare and paid work, and grandmothers' own childcare is substantial")`. Family care in India is best understood as a transfer of time between women of two generations whose terms depend on who the grandmother is and on how the household is arranged, and whose cost falls on older women's rest and leisure.

```

```{r tab-validation}
vt <- validation_table(pd)
i <- vt$Check == "Diaries summing to 1,440 minutes"
vt$Check[i] <- "Diaries not summing to 1,440 minutes"
vt$Value[i] <- paste0(fn(V$n_diaries_not1440), " of ", fn(V$n_diarists))
tab(vt, caption = "Construction and validation of the person-day panel", label = "validation",
    align = c("l", "r"), notes = "All activity records are used; no row sampling. The number of children under six is a direct count of roster members under six.")
```

```{r tab-sample}
sm <- data.frame(
  Step = c("Married women 18--49 at head or junior level, child under six in household",
           "Excluded: head-level women living with a junior married woman aged 15--49",
           "Analysis sample (mothers of children under six)",
           "\\quad with a coresident grandmother", "\\quad junior-level mothers without a grandmother",
           "\\quad head-level mothers without a grandmother",
           "Placebo sample (youngest own child 6--14, no child under six)",
           "Older generation: women aged 45--80", "Older generation: men aged 45--80"),
  N = c(fn(n_u6_pool), fn(n_u6_dropgm), fn(n_my), fn(n_head_gm + n_jun_gm), fn(n_jun_nogm), fn(n_head_nogm),
        fn(n_mp), fn(n_ogw), fn(n_ogm)), check.names = FALSE)
tab(sm, caption = paste0("Sample construction", syn_note()), label = "samplecons", align = c("l", "r"), escape = FALSE,
    notes = "Unweighted counts of person-day diaries. Head level: head or spouse of head. Junior level: married child of head or spouse of a married child.")
```
